articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related Entities, Removes Belarus and North Korea Sanctions, Issues New General Licenses
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 21, 2026. Concurrently, OFAC removed certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea, signaling a recalibration of sanctions policy in these regions.

In addition to the designations and removals, OFAC issued new general licenses pertaining to Iran and Russia. These licenses aim to authorize certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited, providing specific carve-outs for humanitarian aid or other permitted activities.

The agency also published amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) to provide further guidance and clarity on the updated sanctions programs and the scope of the new general licenses. This move is part of OFAC's ongoing effort to ensure compliance and understanding of its complex regulatory framework.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026. These designations target individuals and entities involved in activities that undermine American intellectual property rights.

Alongside these designations, OFAC issued associated General Licenses to mitigate any unintended consequences and to provide authorization for certain transactions that may be incidentally affected. The PAIPA aims to safeguard U.S. innovation and economic competitiveness.
This action underscores the U.S. government's commitment to combating intellectual property theft and holding accountable those who engage in such illicit activities globally.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) on October 16, 2026. This amendment aims to provide updated guidance and potentially expand the scope of authorized activities under the Venezuela sanctions program.

The specific details of the amendment were not immediately disclosed but typically involve adjustments to existing authorizations or clarifications on permissible transactions. Such changes are often made in response to evolving humanitarian needs or diplomatic considerations.

This action follows a recent trend of OFAC adjusting its Venezuela sanctions, including a designation removal earlier in the week, indicating a dynamic approach to the country's complex political and economic situation.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related Entities, Sanctions Cuban Bank, Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and a Cuba designation on October 15, 2026. This action targets individuals and entities involved in Iran's international financial networks and shadow banking activities, as part of 'Operation Economic Outcast.'

Specifically, OFAC imposed blocking sanctions against 16 individuals in Iran and the UAE, and 10 entities—eight in Iran, one in Iraq, and one in Hong Kong. Additionally, the State Department imposed blocking sanctions against Banco Internacional de Comercio, S.A. (BICSA), a Cuban state-owned bank, under Executive Order 14404.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions to provide guidance on authorized transactions and ensure compliance with the updated sanctions.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation on October 14, 2026. This action signifies a potential shift in the U.S. sanctions policy towards Venezuela, possibly in response to ongoing diplomatic efforts or changes in the political landscape.

The individual removed from the SDN List under the Venezuela sanctions program was Jorge Jesús Rodríguez Gómez. Such removals can indicate a de-escalation of tensions or a recognition of changed circumstances regarding the designated individual or entity.
This development follows a period of dynamic engagement with Venezuela, where the U.S. has at times adjusted sanctions to facilitate humanitarian aid or encourage political dialogue.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations on October 13, 2026. These designations target individuals and entities involved in illicit drug trafficking and terrorist financing networks, aiming to disrupt their operations and financial support.

Specifically, OFAC imposed blocking sanctions against four individuals and 11 entities, all in Mexico, for supporting Cartel del Noreste through businesses involved in horse racing, construction, trucking, and the oil and gas sector.
These actions are part of a broader U.S. government strategy to combat transnational criminal organizations and terrorist groups by cutting off their access to the international financial system.

articles.headline: Bank of America Settles with OFAC for $11.6 Million Over Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Bank of America, N.A. on October 13, 2026, totaling $11,662,930. This settlement resolves apparent violations of multiple sanctions programs, including those targeting Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

The apparent violations occurred when Bank of America channeled correspondent banking payments through blocked banks due to technical and human error, allowed designated individuals to make payments and withdraw funds due to poor sanctions alert calibration, failed to promptly update watchlists following OFAC designations, and mishandled business accounts associated with blocked persons due to human error.

This settlement is part of a larger enforcement action by the U.S. Treasury, which also saw FinCEN assess a $1.2 billion penalty and the OCC assess a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America for deficiencies in its anti-money laundering (AML) compliance program.

articles.headline: OFAC Settles with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, Designates International Criminal Court, Removes Burma Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics on October 9, 2026. This settlement addresses apparent violations of OFAC's sanctions regulations, though specific details of the violations were not immediately released.

In a separate action, OFAC designated the International Criminal Court (ICC) and issued associated General Licenses. This designation follows repeated criticism of the ICC's arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and its investigation into the conduct of U.S. troops in Afghanistan.

Additionally, OFAC announced the removal of a Burma-related designation, indicating a potential shift in U.S. policy towards the country or a recognition of changed circumstances regarding the designated entity or individual.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a new Russia-related General License on October 9, 2026. This license aims to authorize certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under the existing Russia sanctions program.

General Licenses are typically issued to provide specific carve-outs for activities deemed permissible, such as humanitarian efforts, certain financial transactions, or the wind-down of operations. This new license may offer relief or clarity for specific sectors or entities impacted by the broad scope of Russia sanctions.

This action follows a period of ongoing adjustments to Russia-related sanctions, reflecting the evolving geopolitical landscape and the U.S. government's efforts to fine-tune its restrictive measures.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related Entities, Issues New Iran-Related and Amended Russia-Related General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 8, 2026. These designations target entities and individuals involved in Iran's illicit activities, further tightening the economic pressure on the regime.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued a new Iran-related General License, which may authorize certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited. Additionally, an existing Russia-related General License was amended, indicating adjustments to the scope of permissible activities under the Russia sanctions program.
These actions underscore the U.S. government's continued focus on countering threats from both Iran and Russia through targeted financial measures and adaptive sanctions policies.

articles.headline: Bank of America Fined $11,662,930 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has been assessed a civil penalty of $11,662,930 by the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on October 13, 2026. This penalty is part of a settlement agreement resolving apparent violations of multiple sanctions programs.

The violations involved processing millions of dollars in payments in apparent violation of sanctions programs targeting Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism. These failures were attributed to technical and human errors, poor sanctions alert calibration, and inadequate watchlist updates.

This OFAC penalty is part of a broader enforcement action by the U.S. Treasury, which also included significant fines from FinCEN and the OCC for Bank of America's deficient anti-money laundering compliance program.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Pays $175,015 OFAC Civil Penalty
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics has agreed to pay a civil penalty of $175,015 to the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on October 9, 2026. This settlement resolves apparent violations of OFAC's sanctions regulations.

The specific details of the violations leading to this penalty were not immediately disclosed in the public record. OFAC civil penalties are typically imposed for breaches of sanctions programs, which can include unauthorized transactions, dealings with blocked persons, or failures in compliance programs.
This enforcement action underscores OFAC's continued vigilance in ensuring compliance with U.S. sanctions laws across various industries, including logistics and shipping.

articles.headline: Individual Fined $1,427,230 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: An individual has been assessed a civil penalty of $1,427,230 by the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on September 10, 2026. This penalty addresses apparent violations of OFAC's sanctions regulations.

While the specific nature of the individual's violations was not detailed in the public announcement, OFAC frequently pursues enforcement actions against individuals who engage in unauthorized transactions with sanctioned entities or jurisdictions, or who facilitate such activities.
This action serves as a reminder that OFAC's enforcement extends beyond corporate entities to individuals who are found to be in breach of U.S. sanctions laws.

articles.headline: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. Pays $60,764 OFAC Civil Penalty
body: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. has paid a civil penalty of $60,764 to the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on August 12, 2026. This settlement resolves apparent violations of OFAC's sanctions regulations.

The details surrounding the specific violations committed by Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. were not publicly elaborated. OFAC penalties are typically issued for non-compliance with U.S. sanctions programs, which can involve a range of prohibited transactions or dealings.
This enforcement action highlights the importance for all companies, regardless of size or industry, to maintain robust sanctions compliance programs to avoid potential penalties.

articles.headline: Federal Reserve and ECB Expected to Hold Rates Steady Amid Inflation Concerns
body: Both the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank (ECB) are widely expected to maintain their current interest rates at their upcoming October policy meetings. This pause comes despite persistent inflation and resilient economic activity on both sides of the Atlantic.

In the U.S., annual Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) inflation stood at 3.4% in August, with core PCE at 3.0%. Euro area headline inflation rose to 3.8%, and core inflation reached 2.5%. The risk of higher energy costs feeding into other goods and services continues to complicate the return to target inflation levels.

While a pause in rate hikes is anticipated, central bank communications suggest that further monetary tightening in December remains a possibility if inflation pressures do not subside. The ECB is also closely monitoring the French debt crisis, which has tightened financial conditions and could influence future policy decisions.

articles.headline: Iran Threatens Regional Economic Targets Amid Rising Oil Prices
body: Iran has reportedly warned the United States and regional nations that it will expand its attacks beyond U.S. military bases and warships to target economic and civilian infrastructure across Gulf states if American and Israeli military strikes resume. This threat comes as Brent crude oil prices were testing $112 per barrel on Thursday.

Iranian officials conveyed these threats through intermediaries, citing airports, oil and gas pipelines, and telecommunications infrastructure in neighboring Gulf states as potential targets. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has also claimed Iran can sever undersea internet cables in the Strait of Hormuz.
These escalating tensions in the Middle East are a significant factor in the elevated global energy prices, with forecasts suggesting Brent crude could remain around $100 per barrel into early 2027.

articles.headline: Deadly Magnitude 7 Earthquake Strikes China's Tibet Region, Killing at Least 16
body: A powerful magnitude 7 earthquake struck a remote area in China's Tibet region on Thursday, October 22, 2026, resulting in at least 16 fatalities, 54 injuries, and the collapse of hundreds of homes. The disaster occurred in Nagqu, a city north of Tibet's capital Lhasa, situated approximately 4,800 meters (5,249 yards) above sea level.

Chinese state media reported that at least 339 homes collapsed, and officials expressed concerns about further building collapses from aftershocks and casualties from rockslides. Search and rescue efforts are being complicated by the challenging geography and low temperatures in the region.

Chinese President Xi Jinping has called for all-out efforts in rescue operations and medical relief work. Communication in some affected areas is down, and local railway authorities have halted trains passing through the region.

articles.headline: Afghanistan Faces Record Hunger and Mounting Human Rights Abuses as Winter Approaches
body: Afghanistan's humanitarian crisis has severely deteriorated in recent months, with the UN reporting record-high levels of acute malnutrition and hunger. As winter approaches, conditions are expected to worsen considerably, compounded by rampant human rights violations, limited access to basic services, and persistent barriers to humanitarian aid.

The United Nations warns that the country is facing an unprecedented crisis, with millions at risk of starvation. The ongoing political instability and economic collapse continue to hinder effective aid delivery and long-term recovery efforts.
International organizations are struggling to meet the escalating needs, calling for increased funding and improved access to vulnerable populations across the country.

articles.headline: Peace Efforts Resume in Geneva to End Sudan's 'Drone War' and Humanitarian Crisis
body: Talks to halt the fighting in Sudan and alleviate the ongoing humanitarian crisis resumed in Geneva on Wednesday, October 21, 2026. Nearly two dozen countries convened to discuss a pathway to a ceasefire and a transition to peaceful governance that represents all Sudanese people.

The conflict, characterized by a 'drone war,' has exacerbated the humanitarian situation, displacing millions and creating severe food insecurity. International pressure is mounting to find a lasting resolution to the protracted violence.
Diplomatic efforts aim to establish a framework for a comprehensive peace agreement, addressing the root causes of the conflict and ensuring the protection of civilians.

articles.headline: OCC Announces Enforcement Actions for October 2026, Including Penalties Against Bank of America and American Express
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released its enforcement actions for October 2026, highlighting significant penalties against major financial institutions. These actions are taken to ensure banks correct deficient practices and comply with regulatory standards.

Among the key actions, the OCC imposed a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A., for deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and sending wires with inaccurate transmittor name information. This marks the largest civil money penalty in OCC history.

Additionally, the OCC issued a cease and desist order and a $350 million civil money penalty against American Express National Bank for deficiencies in its BSA compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and customer due diligence and customer identification program violations.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

articles.headline: OCC Issues Prohibition Order Against Former Fifth Third Bank Teller for Embezzlement
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) issued an Order of Prohibition against Jennifer Hamblin, a former Vault Teller at a Cincinnati, Ohio, branch of Fifth Third Bank, N.A. The prohibition stems from Hamblin's embezzlement of approximately $292,000 in customer funds.

Prohibition orders are issued against institution-affiliated parties (IAPs) to deter, encourage correction of, or prevent violations, unsafe or unsound practices, or breaches of fiduciary duty. These actions reinforce individual accountability for conduct related to bank affairs.
The OCC emphasizes that such measures are crucial for maintaining the integrity of the banking system and protecting consumers from fraudulent activities by bank employees.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

articles.headline: OCC Issues Prohibition Order Against Former U.S. Bank Operations Processor for Embezzlement
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced an Order of Prohibition against Christopher Organista, a former Operations Processor at the La Mirada, California Operations Center of U.S. Bank National Association. The order was issued due to Organista's embezzlement of approximately $194,131 in bank customer funds.

This enforcement action is part of the OCC's ongoing efforts to hold individuals accountable for misconduct within financial institutions. Prohibition orders prevent individuals from participating in the affairs of any bank or other institution as defined by federal law.
The OCC continues to monitor and take swift action against institution-affiliated parties who engage in illegal activities, thereby safeguarding the financial system and public trust.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

articles.headline: BIS Adds Over Three Dozen Entities to Entity List, Focusing on Russia, China, and Burma
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced the addition of more than three dozen companies to its Entity List, effective immediately. This marks the second round of restrictions imposed in as many weeks, targeting entities related to Russia, China, and Burma.

Out of the 37 entities added, 28 are from China, with others from Belarus, Burma, Pakistan, Russia, and Taiwan. These entities are subject to restrictive licensing requirements and policies due to their involvement in activities contrary to U.S. national security or foreign policy interests.

BIS also modified the license review policy of a prominent Chinese university to a presumption of denial, citing its contributions to China's military modernization efforts. This action underscores the U.S. government's continued focus on preventing advanced technology from supporting military advancements in rival nations.

articles.headline: BIS Streamlines Export Controls for Sound Suppressors, Transfers to Commerce Control List
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced that, as of November 20, 2026, the export of certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors will be subject to BIS's Export Administration Regulations (EAR), rather than the State Department's U.S. Munitions List.

This deregulatory action aims to align export controls on suppressors with those already applied to firearms, easing the compliance burden on the firearms industry while continuing to protect national security. Under this new rule, suppressors will be added to the Commerce Control List (CCL).

BIS will now require a license for certain exports, reexports, or in-country transfers of these newly controlled suppressors, including releases of related software and technology to foreign persons. License exceptions currently available for firearms will also be applicable to suppressors.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
